core: Operant conditioning working definition: behavior changes because of what follows it (consequences drive the learning)
Reinforcement increases behavior; punishment decreases it — the two directions
Positive = adding a stimulus; negative = removing a stimulus; the two axes cross into four procedures
The honest note that 'negative' means removal, not bad, and that negative reinforcement is not punishment
Schedules: reinforcement can follow every occurrence (continuous) or only some (partial/intermittent) — no deeper schedule typology
Shaping: rewarding successive approximations (steps) toward a target behavior
Skinner attribution: his work is the classic foundation of operant conditioning
Honest framing: operant conditioning is the everyday behavior ledger — consequences work on everyone
Consequences come after the behavior (timing part of the definition)
supporting: The law of effect (Thorndike) as the historical foundation Skinner built on
Reinforcement is defined by its effect on behavior, not by how pleasant the event is
Partial reinforcement keeps learned behavior going; continuous is fastest for new behavior
outOfScope: Classroom practice and pedagogy (owned by the education subject)
Clinical behavior modification and therapy techniques

claims.claim: Operant conditioning is learning in which behavior changes because of what follows it: behavioral change (learning) occurs as a function of the consequences of behavior.

B. F. Skinner is the classic name associated with operant conditioning; the APA Dictionary credits him as the first to describe it, and he proposed that behavior is motivated by the reinforcements and punishments that follow it.
Reinforcement increases the likelihood of a behavior; punishment decreases it.
Positive procedures add a stimulus after the behavior; negative procedures remove one — and the same add/remove arithmetic applies to both reinforcement and punishment, giving four combinations.

Negative reinforcement is not punishment: it removes, prevents, or postpones an aversive stimulus and thereby increases the probability of the response, whereas punishment (either kind) decreases behavior.

A schedule of reinforcement is the rule determining which instances of a response will be reinforced; continuous reinforcement reinforces every correct response (fastest for new behavior), and partial (intermittent) reinforcement reinforces only some, which keeps learned behavior going.
Shaping produces new forms of operant behavior by reinforcing successive approximations of the target behavior, because an organism rarely produces the full target behavior spontaneously.

The law of effect, first proposed by Edward Thorndike, states that behaviors followed by satisfying consequences are more likely to be repeated and behaviors followed by unpleasant consequences are less likely — the historical foundation Skinner built on.

Operant conditioning extends beyond deliberate training: consequences such as pay, praise, fines, and social responses shape everyday human behavior, as when a student speaks up in class because participation earns points.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Everyday speech blurs 'negative reinforcement' with punishment.
positions: Popular usage sometimes treats any unpleasant consequence as punishment.
In operant conditioning, negative reinforcement removes an aversive stimulus and increases behavior, whereas punishment (positive or negative) decreases behavior.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson follows the technical definitions (APA Dictionary of Psychology; OpenStax Psychology 2e section 6.3) and flags the confusion explicitly in Common Mistakes with an original example (the squeaky helmet strap).

conflictingEvidence.issue: Is a reward the same as reinforcement?
positions: Everyday language treats rewards and reinforcement as interchangeable.
Operant conditioning defines reinforcement by its effect — the behavior increases — so a pleasant event that does not increase the behavior is not functioning as reinforcement for that person.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson defines reinforcement by effect rather than pleasantness and covers the distinction in Common Mistakes.

correctionsNeeded: Replaced the machine-generated generic draft entirely with a source-verified lesson.
Attributed the working definition of operant conditioning and its classic foundation to B. F. Skinner per the APA Dictionary of Psychology and OpenStax Psychology 2e section 6.3.
Stated the positive/negative distinction as add/remove arithmetic with the explicit honest note that 'negative' does not mean bad.

All examples are original to this lesson: the cinema greeter (Leah), the delivery driver's pickup slot (Diego), the scooter-parking notes (Marcus), the pottery posts (Maya), the squeaky helmet strap (Imani), the loading-dock warnings, the weekend console removal (Lin), the gym snack and claw machines (Omar), the swim-coach shaping steps (Coach Reyes and Ana), and the food-truck cashier worked example (Kira).

sourceRecords.title: Reinforcement — APA Dictionary of Psychology
sourceRecords.notes: Read via the APA Dictionary public JSON API on 2026-08-22. Supports reinforcement as a process in which the frequency or probability of a response is increased by its contingency with a stimulus (the reinforcer).

sourceRecords.title: Positive reinforcement — APA Dictionary of Psychology
sourceRecords.notes: Read via the APA Dictionary public JSON API on 2026-08-22. Supports positive reinforcement as an increase in the probability of a response because the response results in the presentation of a stimulus (adding).

sourceRecords.title: Negative reinforcement — APA Dictionary of Psychology
sourceRecords.notes: Read via the APA Dictionary public JSON API on 2026-08-22. Supports negative reinforcement as the removal, prevention, or postponement of an aversive stimulus as a consequence of a response, which increases the probability of that response — and that it is not punishment.

sourceRecords.title: Punishment — APA Dictionary of Psychology
sourceRecords.notes: Read via the APA Dictionary public JSON API on 2026-08-22. Supports punishment as the operant process in which the contingency between a response and a stimulus results in the response becoming less probable. Positive-punishment and negative-punishment entries additionally verified for the add/remove classification.

sourceRecords.title: Shaping — APA Dictionary of Psychology
sourceRecords.notes: Read via the APA Dictionary public JSON API on 2026-08-22. Supports shaping as the production of new forms of operant behavior by reinforcement of successive approximations to the behavior.

sourceRecords.title: Schedule of reinforcement — APA Dictionary of Psychology
sourceRecords.notes: Read via the APA Dictionary public JSON API on 2026-08-22. Supports schedule of reinforcement as the rule determining which instances of a response will be reinforced; the continuous-reinforcement entry confirms reinforcement of every correct response.

sourceRecords.title: Psychology 2e, Section 6.3: Operant Conditioning
sourceRecords.notes: Canonical openstax.org URL; section text read on 2026-08-22 via an Internet Archive capture (snapshot 20210701151940) because openstax.org blocks direct fetch. Supports: operant conditioning as learning to associate a behavior and its consequence; Skinner's proposal that behavior is motivated by reinforcements and punishments; 'reinforcement means you are increasing a behavior, and punishment means you are decreasing a behavior'; the positive/negative add/remove table; continuous versus partial reinforcement; shaping as rewarding successive approximations; and the law of effect (Thorndike) as the historical foundation.

sourceRecords.title: Conditioning and Learning (Mark E. Bouton, University of Vermont)
sourceRecords.notes: Read live on 2026-08-22. Supports instrumental (operant) conditioning as learning to associate actions with their outcomes; the law of effect; effects that increase behaviors as reinforcers and effects that decrease them as punishers; and the everyday human reach of operant conditioning (e.g., participation points shaping classroom behavior).
